name: MAX31865ATP+T
title: RTD-to-digital converter
summary: The MAX31865 turns the resistance of a platinum RTD, PT100 to PT1000, into a 15-bit number read over SPI. A bias voltage drives the RTD in series with an external reference resistor, and a delta-sigma ADC with a 50/60 Hz sinc filter reports the ratio of the two resistances. It accepts 2-, 3- and 4-wire sensors, survives ±45 V on its sensor pins, and flags open, shorted and out-of-range sensor and cable faults. It runs from 3.0 V to 3.6 V and comes in a 20-pin TQFN or SSOP.

circuits.title: 4-wire RTD connection
circuits.description: The RTD is reached over four leads. BIAS drives REFIN+ and the top of RREF; the bottom of RREF ties to REFIN- and ISENSOR, and the same current leaves FORCE+, runs down one lead, through the RTD and back up another lead to FORCE-. Two further leads carry the RTD's own end voltages to RTDIN+ and RTDIN-, so the force-lead resistance stays out of the reading. CI across the two sense inputs filters noise. FORCE2 is grounded and the 3-wire bit stays 0. DVDD and VDD share the 3.3 V rail, each with its own 0.1 µF to ground, and the five logic lines run to the host.

circuits.title: 2-wire RTD connection
circuits.description: The RTD sits on two leads, which suits a sensor close to the converter. FORCE+ and RTDIN+ join at the RTD's top end and RTDIN- and FORCE- at its bottom end, so the lead resistance adds to the reading. The reference string, CI across the inputs, grounded FORCE2, supply bypassing and host lines are those of the 4-wire circuit; the 3-wire bit stays 0.

circuits.title: 3-wire RTD connection
circuits.description: Three leads reach the RTD. FORCE+ and FORCE2 join and drive the top end through the first lead; RTDIN+ senses the top end over a second lead; RTDIN- and FORCE- join at the board and share the third lead to the bottom end. With the 3-wire bit set, the part takes the drop between FORCE+ and RTDIN+ off the measured voltage, which cancels the lead resistance when the leads match. CI sits across RTDIN+ and RTDIN-; reference, bypassing and host lines match the 4-wire circuit.

operation.text: RREF and the RTD are in series, with VBIAS on the top of RREF, so one current flows through both. The drop across RREF is the ADC reference and the drop across the RTD is its differential input on RTDIN+ and RTDIN-; the output code is therefore RRTD/RREF as a 15-bit fraction. Thermistors and other resistive sensors work the same way.

For a platinum RTD the best RREF is four times the sensor's 0 °C resistance: 400 Ω for a PT100, 4 kΩ for a PT1000. For an NTC or PTC thermistor, pick RREF at least as large as the sensor's highest resistance over the range of interest. The recommended RREF range is 350 Ω to 10 kΩ.

Common platinum RTDs read 100 Ω or 1 kΩ at 0 °C. Alpha, the mean slope from 0 °C to +100 °C, is 0.00385 for IEC 751 (PT100) and 0.00392 for SAMA. The curve bends slightly away from a straight line, which the Callendar-Van Dusen equation describes.

A 2-wire RTD reads its lead resistance as part of the sensor, so it works only near the converter: on a PT100, 0.4 Ω in series is about 1 °C of error. A 4-wire RTD separates force and sense leads, removing the lead error. A 3-wire RTD saves one lead: FORCE2 samples the drop between FORCE+ and RTDIN+ and the part subtracts it from RTDIN+ − RTDIN-, which cancels the lead error when the lead resistances match. Configuration bit D4 = 1 selects 3-wire.

The ADC has differential signal inputs (RTDIN+, RTDIN-) and differential reference inputs (REFIN+, REFIN-). A negative input gives code 0; an input above the reference gives full scale. A third-order sinc filter removes 50 Hz or 60 Hz mains and its harmonics by 82 dB; D0 picks the notch. The notch must not be changed while auto conversion runs.

FORCE+, FORCE2, FORCE-, RTDIN+ and RTDIN- withstand up to ±45 V. Analog switches in series with them open when a pin rises above about VDD + 100 mV or falls below about GND1 - 400 mV. During such a fault roughly 350 µA can flow through the protection; it does the part no harm. Fault bit D2 sets and the ADC stops updating until the fault clears, then resumes.

Three kinds of check run. At all times: any protected pin above VDD or below GND1 (bit D2). After every conversion: a result at or above the high threshold (D7) or at or below the low threshold (D6). On request, in a fault-detection cycle: VREFIN- above 0.85 × VBIAS (D5), VREFIN- below 0.85 × VBIAS with the FORCE- switch open (D4), and VRTDIN- below 0.85 × VBIAS with the FORCE- switch open (D3). For the cycle an internal switch can disconnect FORCE- from its GND2 return. Any set fault also sets D0 of the RTD LSB register. Voltages are with respect to GND1.

D7 turns VBIAS on; it may be turned off between conversions to save power and must be on before a 1-shot conversion, and it stays on in auto mode. D6 = 1 converts continuously at the 50/60 Hz rate; D6 = 0 is normally-off mode, from which 1-shot conversions start. D5 = 1 in normally-off mode starts one conversion when CS goes high (after the last byte of a multibyte write) and clears itself. If VBIAS was off, turn it on and wait 10.5 input-filter time constants plus 1 ms before the 1-shot. A single conversion takes about 52 ms with the 60 Hz filter and 62.5 ms with the 50 Hz filter.

Writing 100X010Xb runs the automatic cycle: the ADC goes to normally-off mode and 100 µs delays are inserted before each check so an input filter can settle; D[3:2] return to 00b at the end. When the input filter's time constant exceeds 100 µs, use the manual cycle: with VBIAS on for at least 5 time constants, write 100X100Xb (checks with the FORCE- switch closed, after which it opens and D[3:2] read 10b); wait 5 time constants again and write 100X110Xb (checks with the switch open, then it closes and D[3:2] clear to 00b). Writing 100X110Xb without the first manual step runs the automatic cycle. Setting D5 together with D2 or D3 in one write makes both commands ignored.

Writing D1 = 1 with D5, D3 and D2 at 0 resets fault bits D[7:2]; D1 clears itself. A persisting over/undervoltage sets D2, and D0 of the RTD LSB register, again at once. Fault bits latch until cleared, so intermittent faults are kept.

Registers 01h and 02h hold the 15-bit ratio RRTD/RREF, MSB first, with the Fault flag in D0 of 02h. The high threshold (03h-04h, POR FFFFh) and low threshold (05h-06h, POR 0000h) share that format. A result greater than or equal to the high threshold sets D7 of the fault status register; a result less than or equal to the low threshold sets D6.

SPI modes 1 and 3. The part reads SCLK's level as CS falls to learn the idle clock polarity, so either polarity works. Bits move MSB first in bytes, one clock per bit. The first byte after CS falls is the address: A7 = 0 reads, A7 = 1 writes (reads at 0Xh, writes at 8Xh). Holding CS low continues the transfer and the address increments, wrapping from 7Fh/FFh to 00h/80h. An invalid address reads FFh; writes to read-only registers do nothing. SCLK runs only while CS is low.
A fresh result in registers 01h-02h pulls DRDY low; it goes back high once a read of those registers finishes.

In noisy surroundings a capacitor may go across RTDIN+ and RTDIN-. After an over/undervoltage fault, after a fault-detection cycle, or after VBIAS is turned on, allow at least five filter time constants plus 1 ms before restarting the ADC for specified accuracy.

With 3- or 4-wire sensors, a broken or loose RTDIN+ lead leaves the ADC's positive input floating, so results wander with layout, noise and temperature and may slip past the thresholds. A 10 MΩ resistor from RTDIN+ to BIAS makes such a break read full scale.
An open RTD reads full scale: set the high threshold to catch it, or test on demand for VREFIN- > 0.85 × VBIAS. A shorted RTD reads near zero: set the low threshold to catch it.
Bypass VDD and DVDD each with a 0.1 µF capacitor, ideally a surface-mount ceramic part for low lead inductance and good high-frequency response.
